messages.subject: Is fixing parameter value allowed?
parts:
In one bug example, a parameter's value is fixed.  For a simpler example, 
if data y's are sampled from standard normal, and we modeled them as y ~ normal(alpha + beta, 1). 
Could we use the following syntax in stan?  (It is easy to work around this problem though.)

data {
  int(0,) N;
  double Y[N];
}
parameters {
  double alpha;
  double beta;
}

model {
  alpha <- 0;
  // alpha ~ normal(0.0, 1000); 
  beta ~ normal(0.0, 1000);
  for (i in 1:N)
    Y[i] ~ normal(alpha + beta, 1);
}



-- Jiqiang

Yes, that should be valid, but for some reason, it isn't working now
(for me).

With the model specified as is and using a modified src/models/
normal_estimate/normal_estimate.Rdata file (changed the "y" to "Y"), I
get stuck at 12 iterations of burnin.

When I change the model to have derived parameters, it samples fine.
See modified example below:

data {
int(0,) N;
double Y[N];
}

parameters {
double beta;
}
derived parameters {
double alpha;

}
model {
alpha <- 0;
// alpha ~ normal(0.0, 1000);
beta ~ normal(0.0, 1000);
for (i in 1:N)
Y[i] ~ normal(alpha + beta, 1);
}

I haven't looked into why NUTS is behaving differently for this
example.


Daniel

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: Is fixing parameter value allowed?
parts:
No, fixing a parameter value is not allowed.
There's no gradient, so it doesn't make sense.

The right thing to do is put it in the data block
so it's a constant. Derived parameters are things
that depend on parameters (they may also depend on
other derived parameters and data). Order of ops
matters for derived parameters -- they're executed
in order.

So although Daniel's fix will work -- you can make
a derived parameter fixed -- it's much less efficient
because it requires memory allocation through our
operator new override and also sits on the auto-dif
stack, which we also don't need (it won't hurt anything --
it'll reduce to a no-op that takes time to compute).

A related issue is that we don't treat NA (in the R sense)
data as parameters. The two have to be broken out into
separate arrays. I'm going to write up examples
in the manual that we had on Andrew's board a few
months back

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: Is fixing parameter value allowed?
parts:
Right -- a vector (or usually an array) beta must be
either data or parameter, not a mixture of both.

What Jiaqiang suggests will work if you don't need
beta as a multivariate parameter anywhere, such as
the mean of a multivariate normal or Dirichlet parameter.

For instance, if you need a vector parameter
mu as the mean of a normal, you'd use:

data {
double mu_1; // constant for 1
}
parameters {
double mu[M-1]; // array of params 2:M
}
derived parameters {
vector(M) mu_vec; // vector
mu_vec[1] <- mu_1;
for (m in 2:M) mu_vec[m] <- mu[m-1];
}

You then get M-1 sampled values correspdonding
to the array mu.

I haven't thought about what we can do if the parameters
need to form a simplex, as for a discrete or multinomial
distro parameters.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: Is fixing parameter value allowed?
parts:
This reminds me of an issue that often occurs in practice. We fit a big model and don't understand it, then fit a stripped-down version that runs. Then we want to bridge between the two. A natural way to do this is to gradually "unfix" the fixed parameters using a series of prior distributions, e.g., theta~N(0,.01^2), theta~N(0,.1^2), theta~N(0,1), etc. As I said, it comes up a lot, it's a useful tactic that I haven't seem often discussed (I think Jennifer and I mention it in our book).
A

Masanao and I did just that for the genomics model.

It would also make a nice test case. This may
be another one that's a bit easier for Gibbs

optimization problems.

It reminds me of some of the ways of handling
constraints in optimization that Matt was
telling me about.

- Bob
